nodes.label: Predation management

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_000
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How does the size of juvenile COTS at the diet switch to corals vary in nature?
nodes.answer: The size of juvenile COTS at the diet switch to corals is highly variable in nature.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_001
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What happens to the growth of juveniles when they become coral predators?
nodes.answer: When the juveniles become coral predators, they grow quickly.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_002
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How long can juvenile COTS remain herbivores without coral prey?
nodes.answer: Juvenile COTS can remain as herbivores for at least 6.5 years in the absence of coral prey.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_003
nodes.label: Methods
nodes.question: What method was used to fragment the coral colonies?
nodes.answer: The colonies were fragmented into 2.5-cm-diameter circular cores using a drill press or as 5 cm2 ramets for Acropora cervicornis.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_004
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What maximum size do juvenile COTS reach on an algal diet in the absence of coral?
nodes.answer: On an algal diet in the absence of coral prey, juveniles reach a maximum size of 16-18 mm in diameter.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_005
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What species is the focus of the study discussed in the abstract?
nodes.answer: The focus of the study is on the crown-of-thorns sea star (COTS, Acanthaster sp.).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_006
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the overfishing/predator removal hypothesis regarding adult COTS?
nodes.answer: The overfishing/predator removal hypothesis suggests that adult Crown-of-Thorns Starfish (COTS) have been released from predator control, leading to increased populations.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_007
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How do juvenile COTS choose to switch to a corallivorous diet?
nodes.answer: The switch to corallivory in juvenile COTS may be influenced by interference competition or semiochemicals from conspecific adults.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_008
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What factors influence the timing and size of the diet shift to corallivory among juvenile COTS?
nodes.answer: The timing and size of the diet shift to corallivory varies among juveniles and is influenced by the availability of preferred coral prey and the risk of sublethal predation/damage from coral tentacles.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Predation management_qna_009
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What traits have been traditionally used to characterize the growth of juvenile COTS (Crown-of-thorns starfish)?
nodes.answer: The number of arms and diameter have been used as individual traits to characterize the growth of juvenile COTS.
